notes.meaning: Solomon looked carefully at how God governs the world and saw that the righteous and the wise, along with their actions, are entirely in God's hands. Yet people cannot tell from their outward circumstances whether God is pleased with them or displeased, because both hardship and prosperity happen to all kinds of people. We must trust God's loving care even when we cannot understand how he directs daily events.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Following the Latin Vulgate, this verse is traditionally read to mean that no person knows whether they are worthy of God's love or hatred, pointing to human uncertainty regarding one's own final standing before God.

notes.meaning: The same kinds of earthly events happen to everyone, whether someone is morally upright or wicked, ceremonial and clean or unclean, religious or irreligious. A person who honors God by making vows faces the same basic earthly trials as one who avoids them, and in the end all share the common fate of physical death. God does not use ordinary worldly fortunes to signal who is right and who is wrong.

It is a heavy and troubling reality of life on earth that every person meets the exact same final end in physical death. Because death seems to fall randomly on the good and the bad alike, many people harden themselves in sin and pursue foolish rebellion all their lives. Then, after living recklessly, they pass away and join the dead.

As long as a person is alive, there is still hope for things to improve and an opportunity to turn to God. In the ancient world, dogs were despised scavengers while lions were honored as majestic beasts, yet a lowly living dog is better off than a dead lion. Being alive offers possibilities for repentance and enjoyment that death permanently takes away.

Living people have the advantage of knowing that death is coming, which gives them the chance to number their days and seek wisdom. In contrast, those who have died have no awareness of what happens in this earthly world and can earn no more earthly rewards. As time passes, the living often completely forget the names and achievements of those who are gone.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some groups cite these verses to argue for soul sleep, teaching that human beings lose all conscious existence between death and the resurrection.

notes.meaning: Death brings an end to all the earthly feelings people once held, such as their love, hatred, and jealousy. The dead no longer have any active role or share in the affairs taking place in this world. Their power to help or harm what happens under the sun is finished forever.

notes.meaning: Solomon urges God's people to receive their daily food and drink with a cheerful and grateful heart. Instead of growing anxious over the mysteries of life, believers can enjoy their daily blessings, knowing that God welcomes their quiet faithfulness. Taking joy in simple meals is a good gift from God's hand.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Catholic Douay-Rheims translation renders the second half as 'because thy works please God,' interpreting the joy as springing directly from living a life pleasing to him.

notes.meaning: Wearing clean white clothing and applying soothing oil to the head were ancient signs of festivity, cleanliness, and joy. Solomon encourages an attitude of celebration and gladness rather than walking around in gloom and mourning. God desires his people to live cheerfully and purely during the days they are given.

A husband is encouraged to treasure and enjoy life with the wife he loves throughout his brief years on earth. Life in this fallen world is short and filled with demanding labor, but a faithful, loving marriage is God's special portion of happiness for his people. Cherishing one's spouse brings sweetness to an otherwise fleeting existence.

Whatever good task or duty comes to hand, a person should tackle it with wholehearted energy and diligence. In Sheol, the silent realm of the dead where our bodies go, there is no work, planning, knowledge, or earthly wisdom. Because our time on earth is limited, we must serve God and others today without delay.

Human ability alone does not guarantee worldly success. The fastest runner does not always win the race, the strongest army does not always win the battle, and the wisest workers do not always gain wealth or honor. God's providence permits unexpected moments and surprising circumstances to touch everyone, showing that humans are never in total control.

No one knows when an hour of crisis, trouble, or death will suddenly arrive. Just as fish are unexpectedly trapped in a net while swimming or birds caught in a snare while feeding, people are often taken by surprise when hard times hit. Since life can change in a moment, we should stay humble and rely on God rather than self-confidence.

Solomon shares an example of wisdom in action that made a deep and lasting impression on him. Even though people often overlook wisdom in daily life, he observed an event that showed just how valuable it truly is. True wisdom possesses great worth, even when the world fails to recognize it.

A small town with only a few men inside was attacked and surrounded by a powerful king with a mighty army. The invading king built massive siege ramps against the walls to crush the city. Humanly speaking, the town stood no chance of surviving against such overwhelming force.

Inside the besieged town lived a poor man who possessed great wisdom, and his wise counsel completely saved the city from ruin. However, once the danger was over, the citizens quickly forgot all about this humble man and gave him no honor. Real wisdom can accomplish wonders, even when human gratitude is completely lacking.

This story confirmed to Solomon that quiet wisdom accomplishes far more than mere physical power or military force. Even so, people often look down on a wise person simply because he is poor, and they easily ignore what he has to say. We should value good advice for its truth, not based on the wealth or social standing of the speaker.

The gentle, calm words of a wise person offer far more real help than the loud shouting of a foolish leader. A ruler surrounded by fools may make plenty of noise, but his bluster cannot solve difficult problems. Wise people listen patiently to quiet truth rather than being swept along by loud and arrogant speech.

Wisdom is far more powerful and protective than any weapons of war. Yet a single foolish sinner can quickly destroy a vast amount of good work, tearing down in moments what took great care to build. We should guard our hearts, knowing that one careless sin can do widespread damage.
